The Past Perfect Continuous and Past Perfect Tenses

You use the Past Perfect Continuous to talk about an action that was in progress up to a certain point in the past. You use the Past Perfect to talk about an action that finished before a certain point in the past.

Compare these two sentences:
I had been finishing some work at home when the delivery guy came by, so I didn't hear him leave the package.
I had finished all my work so I started making dinner.
The structure of the Past Perfect Continuous is:
When you want to refer to how many times something happened in the past before another past event, you use the Past Perfect, not the Past Perfect Continuous.

For example:
How many times had you seen the movie before the award ceremony?
I had stayed in the motel twice before.
Marc had been staying at his office longer and longer because his neighbors were noisy and sometimes violent. His life, outside of work, had been becoming uncomfortable.
He had continued on, of course, unhappy but hardworking as ever.
Then something had happened that filled him with amazement.
The date of the last regular street inspection had been exactly fifty years, five months and fourteen days ago.
He had been hoping without hope that such a place might exist. He had been looking for a street where things might be different.
He had been looking for a while before he had found it.
A genial Mrs. Glass  said they had been waiting for someone to find them for years, but no one had.
When you want to report an earlier event, you can use the passive voice. The passive voice puts the emphasis on the receiver of the action rather than the doer (or agent ) of the action.
subject + passive report verb + perfect infinitive
For an event that happened in the past, but reported in the present, you use this structure:

She is believed to never have complimented anyone.
(They believe that she never complimented anyone)
For an event that happened in the past and is reported later in the past, you use this structure:

She was believed to never have complimented anyone.
(They believed that she never complimented anyone)

images.text:
Marc Girondin was believed to have worked in the filing section of the city hall's engineering department for so long that he know every street in the city. No one else was known to have possessed such knowledge. He became the undisputed expert.
Marc had been staying at his office longer and longer because his neighbors were noisy and sometimes violent. His life, outside of work, had been becoming uncomfortable. He had continued on, of course, unhappy but hardworking as ever. He's believed to have spent his 45th birthday alone.
Then something had happened that filled him with amazement. He had discovered an old card he assumed to have been stuck at the back of a drawer for ages. It was labeled GREEN BOTTLE STREET.

The date of the last regular street inspection had been exactly fifty years, five months and fourteen days ago. It was a lost, forgotten street. He had been hoping without hope that such a place might exist. He had been looking for a street where things might be different. The next day he had gone to look at it.
He had been looking for a while before he had found it. The street had been half hidden. He had found six small houses, each with a diminutive garden in front. Windowless brick walls of ancient warehouses had encircled them.

At first glance, Marc realized how it had gotten its unusual name. It was exactly like a bottle in shape. He was entranced! It was just the kind of place he had always wished to have lived in.
He knocked on the door to see if there was a place to rent. When the door opened a Marc explained how he had found the street. A genial Mrs. Glass said they had been waiting for someone to find them for years, but no one had. There had been no tax notices, no water or electricity bills or mail delivered for years.
The street seemed to have been mislaid as it were. Marc decided then and there that it would remain mislaid forever.
